question: A 25-year-old patient sustains an isolated fracture of the shaft of the radius. Which is the MINIMUM immobilisation required to adequately stabilise this fracture in a below-elbow plaster?

answers.text: The wrist joint only, leaving the elbow free

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Immobilising the wrist alone does not control rotation at the fracture site; the forearm bones cross the elbow and rotation occurs at the proximal radio-ulnar joint.

answers.text: The joint above (elbow) and the joint below (wrist) — requiring an above-elbow plaster

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The joint-above-and-below rule mandates that any forearm bone fracture must immobilise both the wrist and the elbow. A below-elbow cast leaves the proximal radio-ulnar joint free and allows rotational movement at the fracture site.

answers.text: The wrist and the finger metacarpophalangeal joints only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The MCP joints are not relevant to controlling a radial shaft fracture. The critical joint to immobilise proximally is the elbow.

answers.text: No joint immobilisation is needed; only padding over the fracture site

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Padding alone provides no fracture stabilisation. The joint-above-and-below principle is fundamental to cast immobilisation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the joint-above-and-below principle. For a radius shaft fracture, the elbow (proximal radio-ulnar joint) and wrist must both be immobilised to prevent rotational displacement.

Well done. The joint-above-and-below rule is a cardinal principle: any fracture of the shaft of a long bone must be immobilised in a cast or splint that spans the joint above AND the joint below the fracture.
